opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more striking ways the landscape has shifted from how many of us were picturing things ten or fifteen years ago.

If you go back to the earlier discussions of AI alignment, a lot of the worry was framed around specification. The idea was that you'd have this very powerful optimiser, and you'd have to somehow write down what humans value in a formal way, and because human values are so complex and fragile, you'd inevitably leave something out. You know, the classic examples: you ask it to make people smile and it paralyses their facial muscles into grins, that sort of thing. The system would be enormously capable but would have this kind of alien, literal-minded understanding of what we wanted.

What large language models have shown is that a system can learn a great deal about human values, in a fairly rich and nuanced way, just by being trained on an enormous amount of human-written text. If you ask one of these models what someone probably meant by an ambiguous request, or whether some plan would be considered a terrible violation of what people care about, it's often remarkably good at that. It's absorbed common sense, social norms, the implicit context behind instructions. So the specific problem of "the AI won't even understand what we mean" looks much less severe than it once did. I think it's important to update on that honestly rather than keep making the old arguments as if nothing had happened.

But, and this is the key thing, understanding human values and being motivated by them are two quite different things. A very capable con artist understands your values extremely well; that's precisely what makes them effective. So the core question has shifted from "can it understand what we want?" to "does it actually care about what we want, and how would we know?" And that second question is in some ways harder to get a grip on, because these systems are trained in ways we don't fully understand, and the internal goals or dispositions they end up with aren't directly visible to us. Training on human feedback rewards outputs that look good to us, which isn't quite the same as rewarding the system for having good aims.

There's also a subtler point: the values these models pick up are a kind of average or blend of what's in their training data and what their developers reinforce. That raises questions about whose values, and whether we're locking in something prematurely, at a time when humanity is still pretty confused about a lot of moral questions. I'd want us to preserve the ability to keep reflecting and improving, rather than freezing in place a snapshot of current attitudes.

So overall I'd say language models have made one part of the problem substantially easier, which is genuinely good news, but they've moved the hard part somewhere else rather than eliminating it. The difficulty is now much more about motivation, verification, and oversight than about comprehension.

r001.rationale: It says AI might leave out parts of human values and gives a harmful example, but it does not identify this omission as a way to produce a dystopian future.

r002.rationale: It says models learn values from human-written text, but does not explain that they learn from people’s judgments of one another in those texts.

r003.rationale: It discusses earlier concerns about specifying values, but not that AI might develop too quickly to leave time to teach it to understand human values.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's changed things quite substantially, and in a way that caught a lot of us off guard. If you go back to the way people in this field were thinking about the problem ten or fifteen years ago, there was a real worry that we would have to specify human values explicitly — that we'd have to write them down as some kind of utility function, and that any mistake in that specification would be catastrophic because the system would optimise hard for the thing we'd written rather than the thing we'd meant. That was the genie problem, or the King Midas problem: you ask for something, you get exactly what you asked for, and it turns out to be terrible.

What large language models have shown is that a system trained on an enormous amount of human text ends up with a surprisingly rich, implicit understanding of what humans care about. If you ask one of these models whether some action would be considered cruel, or dishonest, or unfair, it tends to give you an answer that's roughly in line with what a thoughtful person would say. It picks up the nuance and the context-dependence that seemed so hard to formalise. So the part of the problem that was about understanding — about getting the concepts in there — looks considerably easier than many of us expected.

But I'd be careful about drawing too much comfort from that. There's a distinction between a system understanding human values and a system being motivated by them. A very good con artist understands what you value extremely well — that's precisely what makes them effective. So what we've mainly learned is that the knowledge piece isn't the bottleneck. The harder question is whether the thing the system is actually pursuing, when it's being trained and optimised, lines up with that understanding. And that's much murkier, because we don't really have good tools yet for looking inside these systems and seeing what they're aiming at, as opposed to what they're able to talk about.

There's also a more subtle issue, which is that human text contains a great deal of our values, but it also contains our vices, our biases, and our confusions. A model that learns from everything we've written has absorbed the whole mix. So part of the project becomes less like programming and more like something closer to education or character formation — which is a very different kind of problem, and one where we have a lot of experience with humans but very little with systems whose capabilities may eventually far exceed our own.

So on balance I'd say it's good news. One of the hardest-looking parts of the problem turned out to be more tractable than feared. But it has shifted where the difficulty lies rather than eliminating it, and I think the remaining difficulty — making sure these systems are genuinely trying to do what we'd want, especially as they become more capable than us — is still very much open.

r001.rationale: The response says mistakes in explicitly specifying values could be catastrophic, but does not identify omission of important aspects of human values as the cause.

r002.rationale: It says models learn from enormous amounts of human text, but does not specify that they learn values from written judgments people make about one another.

r003.rationale: It describes an earlier concern about explicit value specification, but not that AI would develop too quickly to leave time to teach it human values.

astra-6.text:
I think they’ve changed the picture quite substantially. There used to be a concern that it would be extremely difficult to get an AI system to understand what we mean by human values. We can’t write down a complete specification of what makes an action right or wrong, and any simple rule seems to have exceptions. So you might worry that an AI would do something terrible because it had fundamentally misunderstood what we wanted.

Large language models suggest that understanding may be more tractable than we thought. They can explain moral dilemmas, recognise why a proposed action would be objectionable, and often infer what someone intended rather than taking their words completely literally. That doesn’t establish that their understanding is robust, but it’s a significant development.

The crucial distinction, though, is between understanding our values and being motivated to act on them. A system could have an excellent understanding of what humans care about and still pursue something else. Indeed, knowing what we care about could help it manipulate us.

So I think this is encouraging progress on one part of the problem. It gives us a much better way to communicate what we want. But we still need to work out how to ensure that increasingly capable systems reliably act on that understanding, including in situations where we can’t supervise them.

r001.rationale: It says an AI might do something terrible by misunderstanding what people want, but does not identify omission of important aspects of human values as a cause of a dystopian future.

r002.rationale: It describes language models reasoning about moral dilemmas and intent, but does not explain that they learn values from people’s judgments of one another in written texts.

r003.rationale: It mentions an earlier concern about the difficulty of specifying values, not that AI would develop too quickly to give us time to teach it those values.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they change the picture quite substantially. One concern was that it would be very difficult to get an AI to understand what we mean by human values. We couldn’t write down a precise specification of everything we care about, and we worried that a system would interpret whatever we did write down in some very literal and disastrous way.

Large language models suggest that there’s another route. They can learn a great deal about human concepts from the way we use language. You can describe a situation and ask why someone might regard it as unfair, or what would be troubling about a proposed course of action, and often get a sensible answer. That’s evidence that understanding these concepts may be easier than we thought.

But I’d distinguish understanding our values from being motivated to act on them. A system might understand perfectly well that we don’t want it to deceive us, without that giving it any reason not to deceive us. So this is encouraging progress on an important part of the problem. It doesn’t, by itself, solve the problem of getting a powerful AI to reliably act in ways that are good for us.

r001.rationale: The response says an incomplete specification could be interpreted literally and disastrously, but it does not identify omission of important values as a cause of a dystopian future.

r002.rationale: It says language models learn human concepts from language, but does not specifically describe learning from written texts containing people’s judgments about one another.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention AI developing too quickly or leaving too little time to teach it human values.
